records.place: Manutuke, by the Te Arai River, Gisborne

wine.name: Millton Te Arai Vineyard Chenin Blanc
wine.sites: The Te Arai Vineyard, the home block on the banks of the Te Arai River near Manutuke, where the house was founded in 1984; autumn mists off the river can bring botrytis in some years.
wine.making: Organically and biodynamically grown fruit is picked by hand in up to four passes through the vineyard, some years ending with a pass for grapes touched by botrytis. The wine is fermented and raised partly in stainless steel tanks and partly in demi-muids, large French oak casks of 600 litres, chosen so that the wood gives texture rather than the taste of oak.
wine.glass: Lime, green apple and quince, with mango in warm years and honey where botrytis has come in; a waxy, textured palate, mouth watering acidity and a softening edge of sweetness on the finish.
wine.ageing: Open and fruity on release; like Chenin Blanc of its weight elsewhere, it can gain honeyed depth over several years in bottle.
wine.serve: 10 to 12 degrees Celsius; no need to decant, though a little air helps a young bottle; a white wine glass of medium size.

label.means: The home block beside the Te Arai River at Manutuke, the wine's single source.
The Geographical Indication of the Poverty Bay region on the North Island's east coast.
The Loire grape, here raised partly in large French oak casks.

records.table: Certified organic in 1989, five years after its founding at Manutuke, Millton Vineyards and Winery draws its Te Arai Vineyard Chenin Blanc from the home block by the river: lime, green apple and honey, a waxy texture and bright acidity, a white for fish.
records.story: The family's roots in Gisborne wine go back to 1969, when the father of one of the founders planted the Opou Vineyard near Manutuke. In 1984 the young couple founded their own winery on the banks of the Te Arai River near Manutuke, on land where, by the house's account, settlers had first planted vines in 1871. They farmed without synthetic sprays from the start, and in 1989 the estate gained organic certification from BioGro, by the accounts of New Zealand Winegrowers and the local press the first wine producer in the country to do so. Biodynamic farming followed, later certified by Demeter, and the house came to be known abroad as a pioneer of both. Chenin Blanc, rare in New Zealand, became its signature: grown on the riverside home block, where autumn mists off the water can bring botrytis, and raised in large casks of the Loire kind. In 2025, after more than forty vintages, the family announced that the harvest of that year would be its last and that it would retire the vineyard and itself rather than sell, so the Te Arai Chenin Blanc stands as the record of one family's work.

Millton is a Gisborne house, not Hawke's Bay or Marlborough: Gisborne lies north of both, on the east coast around Poverty Bay.

records.place: Matawhero, on the Poverty Bay flats, Gisborne

wine.name: Matawhero Gewürztraminer
wine.sites: The home vineyard at Riverpoint on the Poverty Bay flats, planted in the 1960s, on silt loam over clay that gives the grape its rich, dense fruit.
wine.making: Picked while the fruit is cool, often by machine in the early morning, then carried quickly to the winery and pressed, as the house's vintage notes describe. It is made as a fresh, fruit led white in a dry or nearly dry style.
wine.glass: Lychee, nashi pear and Turkish delight with a touch of ginger; a nearly dry palate, rounded in texture and held by a steely line of acidity, with a long, perfumed finish.
wine.ageing: Made for drinking young, in the first few years after the vintage, while its perfume is at its height.
wine.serve: 10 to 12 degrees Celsius; no decanting; a white wine glass with room for the perfume.

label.means: The house's range drawn from named Gisborne vineyard sites rather than a regional blend.
The Geographical Indication of the Poverty Bay region on the North Island's east coast.

records.table: Gewürztraminer made Matawhero's name on the Poverty Bay flats in the 1970s, and the Single Vineyard Gewürztraminer carries it on: lychee, nashi pear and Turkish delight, nearly dry and rounded, with a steely line. Gently spiced dishes suit it well.
records.story: In the 1960s a grower planted a vineyard at Matawhero, on the flats outside Gisborne, importing his own vines, among them Gewürztraminer, a grape then almost unknown in the country. His son brought the family's own label to life in 1975, when the first wines appeared under the Matawhero name, and within a few years his Gewürztraminer was winning notice at home and abroad, so that the house became known for wine of its own rather than for grapes sold on. Through the 1970s and 1980s the name Matawhero and the grape Gewürztraminer went together in the minds of the country's wine drinkers, and Gisborne, long the engine of bulk white wine, had a fine aromatic white to show. In 2008 the son sold the winery and vineyard to a local family, who revitalised and replanted the estate and relaunched the label. They later released the Irwin Chardonnay, of the Mendoza clone the father had brought into the country, named in tribute to the father and son who had founded the house. In 2025 Matawhero marked fifty years since its first wines. Its Gewürztraminer links Gisborne's pioneering years with the wines that came after.

wine.name: Bushmere Estate Classic Chardonnay
wine.sites: The family's own vineyard at Matawhero in the Central Valley of the Gisborne district, on the flats inland from the city, where Chardonnay is the main planting beside smaller plots of Pinot Gris and other grapes; the house's listing with New Zealand Winegrowers gives its Chardonnay as planted in 1972.
wine.making: Fermented in barrel and then matured in French oak, by a merchant's note of the 2024 that agrees with a critic's notes on earlier vintages. The share of new oak, the months in barrel and the extent of the malolactic fermentation vary by vintage and are not given here.
wine.glass: Ripe peach and grapefruit with lemon curd, over vanilla, oak spice, nuts and a touch of toasted brioche; full bodied, with a fresh line of acidity under the fruit.
wine.ageing: Drinks well on release and over the few years after the vintage, while the fruit is generous and the oak fresh.
wine.serve: 10 to 13 degrees Celsius; no need to decant; a wide white wine glass.

records.table: Bushmere Estate is a family vineyard at Matawhero whose Chardonnay goes back, by its own account, to 1972; its Classic Chardonnay is ripe Gisborne fruit fermented and raised in French oak, with peach, lemon curd and vanilla on a full body, so pour it with roast chicken or crayfish.
records.story: Bushmere takes its name, by the house's own account, from old maps of the district, which called this stretch of land at Matawhero, on the flats inland from Gisborne, Bushmere. Chardonnay was planted there in 1972, as the house's listing with New Zealand Winegrowers tells it, at a time when Gisborne was becoming a large supplier of grapes to the country's large wineries, and for decades the family who farm the estate sold their fruit to others rather than make wine of their own. In the middle of the 2000s that trade failed them: Cuisine says their contracts to supply grapes were not renewed, the New Zealand Herald that the winery they supplied would not take all the fruit they had grown. The family answered with a label of their own, founded in 2005 by the regional body Gisborne Wine and by Cuisine; one account dates the cellar door and its restaurant, in a former packhouse on the estate, to 2004. Chardonnay remained the speciality, with smaller plantings beside it, Montepulciano among them, whose 2021 drew praise in a Cuisine tasting of other red varieties in 2024. Its Classic Chardonnay is the wine to know: the generous, ripe and oak touched Chardonnay of the Poverty Bay flats, made by growers who were growing it for others long before the name on the bottle was their own.

records.place: Ormond to Hexton, north of Gisborne

wine.name: TW Chardonnay
wine.sites: The two founding growers' neighbouring vineyards on Back Ormond Road, in the foothills from Ormond to Hexton north of Gisborne, a strip the locals call the Golden Slope after the Côte d'Or.
wine.making: Fermented in barriques of French and American oak, with Hungarian oak in some years, partly with indigenous yeast. The wine then goes through full malolactic fermentation, which gives it its creamy texture, and is fined, stabilised, filtered and bottled, as the house's technical notes describe.
wine.glass: Ripe peach and nectarine with grapefruit, over butterscotch, toasted nuts and vanilla from the barrels; full and creamy, with soft acidity and a long, rounded finish.
wine.ageing: Rich and ready on release; it holds for a few years as the fruit turns nutty, but it is made to be drunk rather than laid down.
wine.serve: 10 to 13 degrees Celsius; no need to decant; a wide white wine glass.

records.table: Barrel fermented and made creamy by malolactic, the Reserve Gisborne Chardonnay of TW Wines, the label two growers began in 1998 to bottle their own fruit, gives ripe peach, butterscotch and toasted nuts; roast chicken or crayfish will match it.
records.story: Gisborne grew Chardonnay for decades before most of its growers made wine of their own, and much of its fruit went to the large wineries. Two growers whose neighbouring vineyards lay on Back Ormond Road, on the foothills the locals call the Golden Slope, wanted a label of their own. In 1997, on a fishing trip to Lake Waikaremoana, they hatched the idea, and they named it simply with the initials of their two families. Advised by local winemakers, they aimed at the next vintage, formed a company, found space in a winery and made their first wines in 1998. The range grew from there: an unoaked Estate Chardonnay, the barrel fermented Reserve, a Chardonnay and Viognier blend, and red wines of Malbec and Merlot. It was built as a small grower's label, a fair picture of a region where the vineyard comes first. In the TW Reserve Chardonnay a guest meets the warm, generous Gisborne style that gave the region its name for Chardonnay.

records.table: For Christmas 1981 Montana launched a sparkling brand named after the painter Gottfried Lindauer, and its core wine, Classic Brut Cuvée, is a dry, non vintage blend of Chardonnay and Pinot Noir, crisp and lemony. Serve it well chilled.
records.story: The name is a painter's. Gottfried Lindauer (1839 to 1926) was born at Pilsen in Bohemia, sailed for New Zealand in 1874 and settled at Woodville, where he painted the portraits of Māori for which he is known; he died there in 1926. In 1981 Montana Wines launched a sparkling wine under his name for Christmas, and the brand grew into a familiar bottle at home and abroad. Montana's own fortunes ran through the sales of the wine trade: it passed to Allied Domecq in 2001 and, with Allied, to Pernod Ricard in 2005. In 2010 Pernod Ricard sold Lindauer, with several other New Zealand brands, to a consortium of Lion Nathan and Indevin; Indevin took the Lindauer winery in Gisborne and the vineyards, and came to make the wine under contract. Montana itself later took the name Brancott Estate, so the two stories part there. The brand's own pages give Gisborne and Hawke's Bay for its Special Reserve and South Australia for the Classic Brut Cuvée. Read the back label, then: a name born in Gisborne need not mean Gisborne fruit.

traps: Lindauer is a brand, not an estate: it has no single vineyard, and its name is a painter's, not a place.
Lindauer began as Montana's brand but left Pernod Ricard in 2010; Brancott Estate, Montana's later name, is a separate house.
The Special Reserve, not the Classic, is the Lindauer the brand describes as bottle fermented with two years on its lees.

report: Pick in doubt, kept: the brand's own Classic Brut page describes a blend of Chardonnay and Pinot Noir from South Australia, while its Brut Cuvée page and a Falstaff listing (Lindauer Classic Gisborne Hawkes Bay Brut Cuvée) give Gisborne and Hawke's Bay. The record follows the latter two; the integrator should confirm which bottle the label means, and a swap to a Gisborne estate (Bushmere Estate or Kirkpatrick Estate) is offered if the Gisborne link is only history.

The method is in conflict: one search summary of the brand's site says many Lindauer wines are made in tank and the vintage wine is the traditional method exception, while an importer and a New Zealand merchant describe the Brut as bottle fermented with twelve to eighteen months on lees. The record says traditional method by those accounts; the checker should settle it.

The launch of 1981 rests on the brand's own Since 1981 and on Tastingbook; the claim that it was the first commercial traditional method wine of the country and the 1980 harvest of Gisborne and Hawke's Bay base wine rest on Tastingbook alone and are left out.
The sale price of 2010 differs by source and is not given; the brand's owners after 2010 are not followed.
Gottfried Lindauer's dates, Pilsen, 1874 and Woodville rest on Te Ara and Wikipedia.
The closing line on Gisborne's role as the source of sparkling base wine draws on the region record and the brand's current Gisborne and Hawke's Bay sourcing; the checker may soften it.
The winemaker named on the brand's site is living and never named.
